To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the extracellular fluid of contracting skeletal muscle is acidic during exercise in a rat model and that this change is consistent with a ventilatory control error signal.
changes in muscle extracelullar fluid pH (pH(e)) can provide an error-signal for exercise ventilatory (respiratory) control.
changes in the pH of the interstitial fluid surrounding contracting muscles can serve as an error signal for ventilatory control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the body regulates its breathing during exercise, a phenomenon known as ventilatory control.
the mechanisms by which the central nervous system controls breathing.

the mechanisms of ventilatory regulation during exercise, specifically the mechanisms by which skeletal muscle afferent information is integrated into the central respiratory control network to regulate the magnitude of the ventilatory response to muscle contraction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pH of skeletal muscle ECF is a candidate for an exercise ventilatory control signal.
the pH error signal for the ventilatory control of exercise is the pH of the interstitial fluid bathing the muscle fibers.
the data are consistent with the hypothesis that changes in pHe of exercising muscle provide an error signal that links skeletal muscle metabolism to ventilatory control.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ventilatory control of exercise is mediated by the interaction of afferent signals from the exercising skeletal muscles and central respiratory neurons.
changes in pHe of exercising muscle are an error signal for ventilatory control, and that the ventilatory response to exercise is mediated in part by a reflex from the muscle to the brainstem.
changes in pHe of exercising muscle can provide a signal for ventilatory control, and the magnitude of the change in pHe is determined by the magnitude of the exercise stimulus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
changes in skeletal muscle extracellular fluid (ECF) pH are sufficient to provide a ventilatory control signal in the setting of exercise.

muscle extracellular fluid acidosis is a candidate signal that can mediate a ventilatory reflex to skeletal muscle exercise in a setting where the central chemoreflex is not activated by arterial pH changes.
changes in muscle pHe may be an important signal for exercise ventilator control.
